extracted.intended_audience: electric cooperative leaders, policymakers (Congress, federal agencies), and co-op stakeholders
extracted.subtask_description: News/advocacy content outlining NRECA's policy positions and asks to federal lawmakers and agencies to protect programs, release funding, and adopt rules that maintain reliable, affordable electric service for co-op members. Covers LIHEAP, USDA/DOE funding programs, EPA rule reviews, permitting reform, and support for always-available generation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protect LIHEAP implementation and staffing
rubrics_metrics.description: Ensure recent staffing cuts at the Department of Health and Human Services do not prevent the agency from administering the Low Income Home Energy Assistance Program (LIHEAP).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: NRECA and APPA urged Senate leaders to rigorously oversee HHS so elimination of staff from the energy assistance division 'does not mean that LIHEAP comes to a halt.' They requested that HHS release about $400 million in remaining LIHEAP money appropriated to states for fiscal year 2025, noting 'time is of the essence' for cooling assistance as summer approaches.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timely release and use of LIHEAP funds
rubrics_metrics.description: Release appropriated LIHEAP funds promptly so assistance reaches consumers rather than remaining at the U.S. Treasury.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failure to release funds in a timely way 'will mean that life-saving assistance dollars will sit at the U.S. Treasury rather than keeping service flowing uninterrupted to Americans in need.' LIHEAP funds are typically paid directly to utilities as bill credits for approved applicants.

rubrics_metrics.name: LIHEAP eligibility and benefit targeting
rubrics_metrics.description: Both renters and owners are eligible for LIHEAP as long as they are responsible for paying utility bills; higher benefits go to households with the greatest home energy needs relative to income and household size.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Program design: consumers apply through local LIHEAP offices, approved applicants receive credits on their energy bill with funds paid directly to the utility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Support for executive actions that protect reliability and affordability
rubrics_metrics.description: Back executive measures that grant temporary regulatory relief or use emergency authorities to keep power generating units operating and preserve always-available resources.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples cited include a proclamation to grant temporary exemptions from the mercury and air rule for coal plants, executive orders directing the Energy secretary to use emergency authorities to keep units operating, actions targeting certain states' renewable portfolio standards, and support for coal mining and production. NRECA frames these as linked to co-ops' message about the need for reliable, affordable power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use regulatory exemptions when standards are infeasible or threaten reliability
rubrics_metrics.description: Authorize temporary exemptions from rules (e.g., the mercury and air rule) if required technology is unavailable and exemptions are in the national security interest to avoid premature plant closures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Clean Air Act permits presidential exemptions where technology cannot meet standards; NRECA argues such exemptions prevent retirements that would threaten reliability. The mercury and air rule 'requires a 67% cut in filterable particulate matter' but does not identify cost-effective technologies to meet that goal, so exemptions can avert forced retirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preserve always-available, dispatchable generation to ensure fuel security
rubrics_metrics.description: Maintain capacity from coal, natural gas, and nuclear plants—'always-available' resources—to meet growing demand and provide reliable baseload power.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: NRECA and co-op leaders argue that closing dispatchable units risks reliability; examples include coal units that provide 24/7/365 generation and plants with on-site fuel stores (e.g., '50+ days of fuel stored on site' at Plant Scherer). The approach is described as 'resource-neutral' but emphasizing the importance of dispatchable resources.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advocate EPA rule reviews that avoid forcing premature retirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Ask EPA to review and reconsider rules (power plant greenhouse gas rule, mercury and air rule, ozone transport rule, power plant wastewater rule, coal ash program) to ensure they are lawful and do not jeopardize reliable, affordable electricity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: NRECA flagged concerns in a letter and met with EPA leadership; it frames rule reconsideration as a 'critical step' toward a more reliable and resilient grid and accuses certain rules of mandating unproven technology and unachievable emissions limits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expedite release and efficient administration of USDA energy funding (New ERA, PACE, REAP)
rubrics_metrics.description: Move quickly to release previously obligated USDA funding under New ERA, PACE, and REAP so co-ops can proceed with projects that modernize systems and provide reliable power.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Secretary Rollins gave co-ops 30 days to review and make voluntary changes to align projects with law and policy; New ERA/ PACE/REAP provide grants and low-interest loans for generation, storage, PPAs (e.g., Palisades nuclear restart), SMR development, and carbon capture projects. NRECA said these programs 'provide important tools for co-ops to invest in their systems.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Ensure federal programs supporting co-op projects operate efficiently and effectively
rubrics_metrics.description: Federal programs and resources that support electric co-op energy projects should be administered efficiently so awarded projects can proceed and investments are realized.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: NRECA warned that without DOE funding 'many of these projects would not be affordable for our members' and urged that programs be run to enable co-ops to move forward with awarded grants and loans.

rubrics_metrics.name: Support DOE infrastructure programs that bolster grid resilience
rubrics_metrics.description: Use DOE infrastructure funding and programs (e.g., WARN, START, microgrid consortium) to implement projects that harden the grid, reduce outages, and improve transmission and resilience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: WARN grants for wildfire mitigation, START consortium projects with advanced overhead conductors to increase transfer capacity, microgrid projects to ensure adequate power when capacity is tight. These projects 'will enhance grid resilience, reduce outages, meet increasing electricity demand, and keep costs low for our rural consumer-members.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Permitting reform and cutting bureaucratic red tape
rubrics_metrics.description: Reform environmental permitting and reduce litigation delays so co-op infrastructure projects can be built and maintained without prolonged delays.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Calls include speeding environmental and historic preservation reviews, allowing greater applicant involvement, curbing lengthy costly litigation, and 'cutting red tape' as necessary to avoid crippling delays that threaten projects and community vitality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protect access to federal incentives such as direct-pay tax credits
rubrics_metrics.description: Congress should protect co-ops' access to direct-pay tax credits and other federal incentives that enable investment in innovative infrastructure projects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: NRECA asks Congress to support USDA and co-ops deploying projects and 'oppose any cuts to the New ERA program,' while noting investor-owned utilities long benefited from tax incentives and co-ops need parity to leverage federal incentives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prioritize diverse energy portfolios and local-appropriate technologies
rubrics_metrics.description: Support a balanced approach that includes all available energy sources and local-appropriate technologies (natural gas plants, renewables repowering, transmission upgrades, storage, SMRs, carbon capture) to meet escalating demand and local needs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Basin Electric and other co-ops highlighted planned investments—new gas plants, wind repowering, transmission projects—to ensure reliable, affordable, and environmentally responsible energy. Projects should be chosen to meet local load growth and economic development needs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value projects that create jobs and strengthen regional energy security
rubrics_metrics.description: Favor projects (e.g., carbon capture, nuclear restarts, PPAs) that strengthen U.S. energy security, create jobs, and support economic growth in energy-producing regions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include Minnkota's Project Tundra (4 million tons/year CO2 capture), Palisades nuclear plant restart via PPAs, and New ERA-funded projects that together 'will unleash over 13 GW of energy in rural communities.' NRECA frames these projects as helping 'realize the Trump administration’s goal of American energy dominance.'
